A 1500 year long record of river discharge, inferred from fluviate-marine sediments from Moreton Bay in east Australia, shows a shift in the frequency of 'dry' El Nino events and a hemispheric-scale broad cooling trend from 600 to 1200 CE, and a broad increase in discharge from 1300 to the present.
the relative freshwater input from the catchment into Moreton Bay was lower between 630 and 1200CE, especially between about 1100 and1200CE.

(i) the Moreton Bay record shows that the last 100 years of the instrumental record is not representative of the full range of hydroclimate variability in the region over this period, and (ii) the record indicates that the last 500 years of the instrumental period is characterized by a prolonged wet period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the past and current climate of the Australian subtropies.
the reconstruction of past hydroclimates, and the implications of this for the management of water resources and climate change.
the reconstruction of past climate variability, with a focus on the last millennium in the Australian subtropical region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there has been a long-term increase in the frequency of dry El Nino events in the austral Pacific over the last 1500 years.
the Moreton Bay record indicates that freshwater discharge to the bay was lower between 630 and 1200 CE, and increased after 1300 CE.

this study provides evidence of a prolonged period of low freshwater discharge from 630 to1200CE and a subsequent increase to the present day, which is consistent with the broader hemispheric climate trends of the Little Ice Age and the Medieval Warm Period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
this study provides a new perspective on the natural variability of climate in Australia over the last ~1000 years.
this paper provides a high resolution record of hydroclimate variability for the last 1500 years in the Australian subtropical region.

this study demonstrates that fluvial-marines sediments can be used to reconstruct hydroclimate variability in the Australian subropics, and that this variability was not only driven by the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, but also by the Indian Ocean Dipole, the Southern Annular Mode, the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, and the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hydroclimatic variability of the past 1500 years has been greater than the instrumental record suggests, with periods of prolonged wetness and drought.
the instrumental record does not cover the full extent of natural climate variability in the region, and that the instrumental record is not necessarily a reliable proxy for future climate.

, while the instrumental record is a useful tool for assessing the impacts of climate change on the environment, we should not rely on it alone to inform our understanding of climate change and the environment.
